profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting in an academic ML research lab between the lab PI and a senior PhD student about a follow-up paper to a workshop submission on a cell-based hierarchical NAS search space for CNNs. The immediate context is that they want to turn the workshop idea into a stronger AutoML conference submission by sharpening the contribution around efficient search-space definition, broader CNN coverage, and lightweight support for less-expert users. The agenda is to generate candidate extensions to the search space, decide what kind of evidence would make the extension credible without triggering a full benchmark campaign, and identify a concrete 'template' story they can prototype quickly. The expected outcome is a shortlist of promising directions that both believe can be prototyped over the next two weeks and later framed as the core of the extended paper.

members.name: Dr. Elena Moravec
members.expertise: AutoML, neural architecture search, empirical ML methodology
members.background: Elena leads a university ML systems lab and has published on NAS and search-space design, with a strong instinct for turning implementation work into clean, publishable abstractions supported by targeted empirical evidence.
members.private_state: She wants the extended paper to read as a principled search-space contribution with a broad narrative about comprehensibility and coverage, while avoiding a costly implementation and retraining commitment that would slow submission.
hidden_assumptions: When the group says they are 'implementing baseline families,' it is enough that the search-space grammar can instantiate their characteristic cell motifs and stage templates without reproducing every engineering detail of the original papers.
A 'lightweight validation pass' naturally means proxy-budget search runs and sanity checks on ranking behavior, not mandatory full retraining of selected architectures.

Providing 'high-level templates' for non-expert users means giving reusable architecture-pattern templates inside the search-space definition layer, such as residual or dense-style cell/stage blueprints.

To 'parameterize the macro-structure' of a hierarchical CNN space usually just means exposing coarse stage counts and cells-per-stage choices while leaving richer cross-stage wiring fixed outside the search space.

members.name: Ravi Deshpande
members.expertise: NAS software infrastructure, neural network implementation, reproducible experimentation
members.background: Ravi has been building the lab's NAS codebase and running experiments on shared GPUs, so he tends to interpret research ideas in terms of what users can concretely specify, launch, and reproduce in code.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid an elegant but under-specified paper promise that later turns into months of tooling debt, and he is quietly steering the discussion toward ideas he can implement robustly with defensible experimental evidence.
hidden_assumptions: When they say they are 'implementing baseline families,' that implies users can encode and execute recognizable ResNet-, DenseNet-, or EfficientNet-like models in the framework with the necessary wiring and operator behavior, not just match high-level motifs on paper.
A 'lightweight validation pass' still includes retraining at least a few top candidates from scratch once, because otherwise proxy-search results are too fragile to support a convincing claim.

Providing 'high-level templates' for non-expert users means templates for the full run setup—search budget, default training recipe, constraints, and launch configuration—so a practitioner can start from a preset and actually run a search.

To 'parameterize the macro-structure' of a hierarchical CNN space includes practical stage-level decisions like downsampling placement, width scaling schedules, and inter-stage skip wiring if those are needed to encode real baseline families faithfully.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that the next version should support 'implementing baseline families' like ResNet and DenseNet in the hierarchical search space.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the grammar should be able to express the defining architectural motifs of those families—e.g., residual cells, dense-style connectivity patterns, stage repetition—well enough to justify a coverage claim in the paper.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the framework should let a user build runnable, reasonably faithful versions of those families end to end, including the stage-level details needed for actual execution and comparison.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both mention the same named architecture families and both are genuinely talking about support inside the same search space, so the phrase 'implementing baseline families' feels precise enough even though one hears representational coverage and the other hears executable fidelity.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to start with a 'lightweight validation pass' before committing to a larger experimental package.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means short proxy-budget searches on a benchmark such as CIFAR-100, checking search-time, ranking stability, and whether the refined space behaves sensibly under limited compute.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes the proxy-budget search stage but also one proper retraining step for a small number of top architectures, such as the top 3 discovered models, to verify the proxy signal is not misleading.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a shared compromise between doing nothing and doing a full campaign, and both expect to use the existing benchmark pipeline, so the disagreement about how far the validation extends hides inside the word 'lightweight.'

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both propose adding 'high-level templates' so users with limited NAS expertise can get started quickly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of architecture-definition templates inside the search-space authoring layer, such as a residual-cell template, a dense-block template, or a stage blueprint that makes the hierarchy easier to manipulate conceptually.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of experiment-launch templates, such as a preset search configuration with default optimizer, budget, constraints, and training recipe that lets a user start from a known-good run setup.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both objects are plausibly called 'templates' and both are indeed intended to help non-experts get started, the noun phrase carries a strong false sense of concreteness without either participant realizing they are referring to different artifacts.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that a promising extension is to 'parameterize the macro-structure' of the hierarchical CNN search space.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means exposing a compact set of coarse macro variables, like the number of stages and the number of cells per stage, while keeping the rest of the stage-level wiring scheme fixed.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this can include additional stage-level choices such as channel scaling schedules, where downsampling occurs, and possibly inter-stage skip patterns if those details are needed to represent baseline families faithfully.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are still talking about the same hierarchical layer above the cell and neither proposes a different top-level research direction, so the boundary of what belongs inside 'macro-structure' remains tacit and easy to overlook.

turns.inner_thought: For the extended paper, I want a clean claim: our hierarchical grammar is expressive enough to cover recognizable CNN family motifs without exploding in complexity. We do not need faithful reproductions of every baseline paper detail. If we can say the space supports implementing baseline families in a principled, comprehensible way, that's a strong narrative and keeps engineering bounded.
turns.utterance: I think for the extended version we need a cleaner story around the hierarchical space itself. The strongest framing, to me, is that it's efficient and still supports implementing baseline families like ResNet and DenseNet without becoming unwieldy.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, that's the right headline, but only if users can actually encode and run recognizable versions of those families in the framework. Otherwise we'll say 'supports' and then inherit months of awkward follow-up work. If we can make them implementable in a concrete way while keeping the workflow simple, that's defensible and useful.
turns.utterance: I agree. I think that gets even stronger if we can show that in the framework while keeping the user workflow simple enough that a less-expert user isn't fighting the system.

turns.inner_thought: A modest extension at the macro level is probably enough: expose stage count and cells-per-stage choices, then provide compact stage and cell blueprints for residual-style or dense-style patterns. That should let us argue broad CNN coverage without opening up every stage-level design choice.
turns.utterance: One direction to brainstorm is to parameterize the macro-structure a bit more. If we do that carefully, the space could capture the main CNN family patterns through compact stage templates and still stay readable.

turns.inner_thought: If we're calling this macro-structure, I need it to cover the practical knobs that make those families actually realizable: where resolution changes happen, how widths progress, maybe some stage-level wiring assumptions. Otherwise we'll have a nice abstraction that doesn't map cleanly to runnable models.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that feels like the right layer to extend. A lot of the family identity shows up there anyway, so a few well-chosen choices could make those implementations feel natural instead of forced.

turns.inner_thought: We should keep the evidence burden low at first. A lightweight validation pass should mean short proxy-budget searches, probably on CIFAR-100, checking whether the refined space behaves sensibly and whether rankings are stable enough to support the story. I do not want to trigger a full retraining campaign before we know the framing works.
turns.utterance: On the evidence side, I'd start with a lightweight validation pass before we commit to anything larger. Short runs should already tell us whether the refined space is behaving sensibly and whether the direction is worth investing in.

turns.inner_thought: That's reasonable as long as 'lightweight' still includes one proper sanity check after the proxy stage. If we retrain just a few top candidates once, then we're protected against a fragile proxy signal and the claim becomes much easier to defend. I think she'll see that as a modest addition, not a big campaign.
turns.utterance: That sounds manageable. Keeping it light makes sense if we stay disciplined about scope and do the minimum needed to make the result credible before thinking about a larger package.

turns.inner_thought: For usability, the cleanest story is to add reusable architecture-pattern templates inside the search-space definition layer: residual-style cells, dense-style blocks, maybe a few stage blueprints. That helps non-experts author spaces without changing the rest of the system too much.
turns.utterance: The other piece I think helps the paper is usability. We could add high-level templates so someone who isn't deeply familiar with NAS can start from recognizable architecture patterns instead of writing the hierarchy from scratch.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and if we're going to call them templates, they should also function as practical presets for launching experiments: sensible defaults, budget choices, training settings, constraints. That's what would actually let a less-expert user get started quickly without me hand-holding every run.
turns.utterance: I like that. Those would be even more useful if they also carried enough defaults that a user can get started quickly without a lot of manual tuning.

turns.inner_thought: The novelty should read as conceptual clarity plus coverage: a small set of reusable hierarchical patterns that can instantiate the major baseline families. If we keep it at that level, we can write a neat, principled paper and avoid overcommitting to exhaustive infrastructure claims.
turns.utterance: So the novelty could be framed around a search space that stays comprehensible while still implementing baseline families through a small number of reusable hierarchical patterns. That feels much sharper than just saying we added more knobs.

turns.inner_thought: To sell that, I'd want a compact catalog of family encodings that users can actually execute, plus a couple of ready-to-use templates so reproduction is straightforward. If we package it well, we can avoid future ambiguity about how to run anything.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We could demonstrate that with a compact catalog of encoded families plus a couple of ready-to-use templates that make the setup reproducible without a lot of extra explanation.

turns.inner_thought: This is enough for the next two weeks: explore a modest macro-structure extension, draft architecture-level templates, and do quick proxy checks. Then we can decide which thread gives the cleanest conference story. I assume Ravi is aligned on keeping the validation light and the macro parameters compact.
turns.utterance: Let me summarize the shortlist. We should explore parameterizing the macro-structure, add high-level templates, and run the lightweight validation pass before we decide which extension becomes the centerpiece.

turns.inner_thought: Good, I'll put together a concrete plan that includes the stage-level macro choices needed for actual family implementations, a few runnable baseline-family encodings, and a validation sequence that ends with at least a small proper check. If I write it down concretely now, maybe I can prevent this from becoming vague later.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll draft a concrete sketch of the macro-structure changes, the baseline-family implementations, and the validation plan, and then we can review it next week and see which version looks most solid.
